title: [Chapitre] I. Vers une géométrie des formes (topologiques) : notes manuscrites (05/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
This page finishes an axiomatic description of the one-dimensional building block of Grothendieck's 1986 'géométrie des formes (topologiques)'. That project is a combinatorial or tame replacement for point-set topology, in the spirit of the 'topologie modérée' of the Esquisse d'un programme.

On the previous pages, a model of 1-form L whose boundary is ∂L = {x0, x1} carries an order relation with the following features:
- x0 is the least element and x1 the greatest.
- The sub-segments are exactly the I_{x,y} with x<y, with closure {z : x≤z≤y} and boundary {x,y}.
- The order is infinitely divisible: x<y implies there is z with x<z<y.
- It is locally filtrant: x<y1,y2 implies there is y with x<y≤y1,y2. Dually it is locally cofiltrant, so 'locally bifiltrant'.
- Conversely, such an order defines a structure of model of 1-form, more precisely of 1-segment, with ∂L = {x0, x1}. The opening line of this page completes that converse.

The page then removes the choice of origin. Exchanging x0 and x1 replaces the order by its opposite. Divisibility and local bifiltration are self-dual conditions. Hence an (unoriented) segment-model structure on L is the same as a 'bi-order', an unordered pair {≤, ≥} of mutually opposite orders, such that for each (equivalently one) of the two orders:
- there are a least and a greatest element, and they are distinct (L is not the one-point model);
- the order is divisible (dense);
- the order is locally filtrant and locally cofiltrant.

The next page defines an orientation of the segment as the choice of one endpoint, equivalently of one of the two orders. It then applies this to regular models to define π0 (connected components) via the equivalence relation generated by 'x and y lie in a common segment'.

In modern terms: an unoriented segment is a bounded dense order considered up to reversal, essentially a betweenness structure. No completeness or countability is required, so for example [0,1]∩Q qualifies. This fits the combinatorial, 'tame' spirit of the project rather than modelling the real interval.
errors: Possible gap: totality of the order is never stated, and the explicit local filtrant/cofiltrant conditions would be automatic for a total order. That suggests a partial order is intended. But the listed conditions (least and greatest elements distinct, dense, locally filtrant and cofiltrant) do not force totality. Counterexample: take two copies of [0,1] identified on [0,1/2)∪(3/4,1]. Order points by real value, with points of the two distinct branches over [1/2,3/4] incomparable. This order is transitive, bounded, dense, and locally filtrant and cofiltrant. Yet it has incomparable elements, so it is a 'bubble' with two paths from x0 to x1 rather than a segment. So either totality, or extra axioms from the ambient notion of 1-form, must be assumed for the 'équivaut' to hold.
Minor: the 'one point' exclusion is written ambiguously (Card L > 1 versus L ≠ point). With least ≠ greatest it is automatic in any case.

ideas.what: Unoriented segment = pair of mutually opposite orders (bi-order) satisfying self-dual axioms; orientation = choice of one of the two orders / one endpoint
ideas.modern_name: betweenness relation / order up to reversal; orientation of an interval
ideas.usually_credited_to: classical (Pasch, Huntington on betweenness, early 20th c.)

ideas.what: Axiomatization of a 1-segment model as a bounded, dense, locally bifiltrant order (no completeness required)
ideas.modern_name: bounded dense (linear) order; combinatorial model of an interval in tame topology
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cantor (dense orders); tame/o-minimal topology (van den Dries et al.) for the general philosophy
ideas.where_published: Only the general programme of 'topologie modérée' appears in Esquisse d'un programme (1984); this specific axiomatics is not there to my knowledge

ideas.what: Self-duality of the axioms (divisibility, local bifiltration) under order reversal

missed.claim: As written, the order-theoretic characterization of a segment omits totality. The local filtrant/cofiltrant conditions suggest Grothendieck meant to allow partial orders and believed the conditions suffice. A 'bubble' poset (two branches glued on initial and final open-ish parts) satisfies all stated axioms but is not a segment. This is a small gap in an unpublished foundational sketch, not a new result.
missed.quote: une structure de modèle de segment équivaut à une structure de bi-ordre (paire d'ordres opposés) qui soit telles que pour chacun (ou l'un) des ordres qui la composent, il y ait un plus petit et plus grand élément distincts ... divisible, et loc^t filtrante et cofiltrante
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of interest to anyone reconstructing Grothendieck's 'géométrie des formes' as a combinatorial alternative to topology. It shows the axioms need a totality or no-cycle condition, presumably supplied elsewhere by the 1-form axioms.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is an elementary reformulation of a segment as a bounded dense order up to reversal, with orientation as the choice of order. It documents the foundational style of the unpublished 'géométrie des formes', but contains no new mathematics beyond a minor axiomatic gap.
transcription_corrections: 'donc la relation d'ordre est remplacée' — the word may be 'dans' or 'alors'; meaning unchanged.
'pour l'un[?] {+(ou l'un)[?]+} des ordres' is more likely 'pour chacun (ou l'un) des ordres qui la composent'.

'(in[?] [-Card-] L > 1 — un point, cas L = ∞[?])' is likely '(i.e. [Card crossed out] L ≠ 1 — un point, cas L = e[?])': it excludes the one-point model; the symbol after 'L =' is uncertain and probably not ∞.
The first line ends 'de 1-forme,' and the next is '{plus précisément, de 1-segment},' — the braces are Grothendieck's own.
